newsitem.title: USA: International finance ministers launch debt plan.
newsitem.headline: International finance ministers launch debt plan.

text.p: International finance ministers launched a debt relief initiative on Monday that is meant to bring economic growth to the world's poorest countries, mainly in Africa.

The initiative, which was endorsed by the joint Development Committee of the World Bank and International Monetary Fund, aims to lift the burden on countries that must spend the benefits of economic growth servicing their debts.
"This is a breakthrough," World Bank President James Wolfensohn told reporters. "It was very good news for the poor of the world."
IMF Managing Director Michel Camdessus said work will begin immediately on identifying which countries will benefit first from the plan, and by how much.

The IMF and the World Bank had tentatively identified a list of up to 20 countries that seem to be the most in need of help, but both Camdesuss and Wolfensohn stressed Monday they would go ahead on a case-by-case basis without preconditions.
The IMF chief said, though, that Uganda would likely be among the first to benefit from the multi-year plan.
Other countries that might eventually benefit include: the Ivory Coast, Ethiopia, Guyana, Bolivia, Mali, Burkina Faso, Guinea Bissau, Mozambique, Sao Tome, Sudan, Zaire and Zambia.
The initiative, which would involve action by creditor countries, the IMF and the World Bank, is expected to cost up to $7.7 billion.

On Saturday, the Paris Club of creditor countries said it was willing to write-off up to 80 percent of debt owed by low-income countries on a case-by-case basis compared to 67 percent currently available under so-called Naples terms.
That is short of the 90 percent write-off advocated by the World Bank and the IMF.

But Wolfenbsohn said that he was not concerned that some countries would fall through the cracks as a result and voiced confidence that the Bank, the IMF and the Paris Club would be able to work out any differences when the time arose.
Oxfam International, an environmental and development group, welcomed the decision to launch the initiative.

"It could bring down the curtain on a debt crisis which, apart from reinforcing economic problems, has been undermining the access of poor people to primary health, basic education and clean water and sanitation," Oxfam representative Justin Forsyth said.

U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin said on Sunday he expected the new debt relief initiative to prove as important for poor nations as the 1989 Brady plan was for middle-income developing countries.
That debt-reduction plan, named after former U.S. Treasury Secretary Nicholas Brady, helped restore the economies of many Latin American countries to good health.
In formally launching the debt initiative on Monday, finance officials left open a number of questions about its financing that will ultimately have to be dealt with.
The IMF's policy-making Interim Committee pledged on Monday to find the money it needs to participate in the plan, but stopped short of spelling out where it would come from.

The decision, announced in a communique issued after a day of talks, effectively left unanswered the question of whether the IMF will eventually sell off some of its gold to finance stepped-up aid for the world's poor.
Also unanswered is the question of where the cash-strapped African Development Bank, which is also supposed to participate in the plan, will find the money to take part.
